concepts.title: Why airspace is divided
concepts.explain: The FAA divides airspace into regulatory and nonregulatory categories. The operational types include controlled, uncontrolled, special-use and other airspace.
concepts.apply: Before every flight, identify the class at each planned altitude and the rules for the route.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 15 — Figure 15-1

concepts.title: The airspace profile
concepts.explain: An airspace profile shows overlapping vertical and lateral boundaries. A position may be under Class B, inside Class E, or in Class G depending on altitude and location.
concepts.apply: Read both the charted floor and ceiling; one airspace label never describes every altitude.

concepts.title: AGL and MSL
concepts.explain: AGL is height above the ground. MSL is altitude above mean sea level. Airspace boundaries may use either, and Class A uses flight levels.
concepts.apply: Do not confuse a 700-foot AGL Class E floor with 700 feet indicated altitude.

concepts.title: Rules follow your actual position
concepts.explain: Airspace class determines weather minimums and may dictate clearance, communication and equipment requirements. A horizontal move or climb can change your obligations.
concepts.apply: Plan your route in three dimensions, including climb and descent.

check.question: Airspace class can change when you...
check.explanation: Airspace boundaries have both vertical and horizontal limits.

concepts.title: Typical Class A boundaries
concepts.explain: Class A generally begins at 18,000 feet MSL and extends through FL600 over the contiguous United States and adjoining specified waters.
concepts.apply: Transition pressure altitude procedures and flight levels belong in the high-altitude planning picture.

concepts.title: IFR operations
concepts.explain: Class A operations generally require instrument flight rules, an IFR clearance and an appropriately rated and equipped flight crew and aircraft.
concepts.apply: A private pilot flying only VFR cannot simply climb into Class A.

concepts.title: Flight levels
concepts.explain: In the U.S., flight levels use the standard altimeter setting of 29.92 inHg. FL180 corresponds to a pressure altitude of 18,000 feet.
concepts.apply: Use correct altimeter-setting procedures when entering or leaving the flight levels.

concepts.title: Check current rules
concepts.explain: Class A boundaries, equipment requirements and exceptions are established by regulation and current aeronautical publications.
concepts.apply: Do not rely on an approximate diagram for an ATC clearance.

check.question: Which is normally required for operations in Class A?
check.explanation: Class A is generally IFR airspace.

concepts.title: Layered shelves
concepts.explain: Class B is individually designed around major airports, generally from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL, with shelves of different floors.
concepts.apply: A route passing beneath a shelf may remain outside Class B even when close to the main airport.

concepts.title: Explicit ATC clearance
concepts.explain: To enter Class B, you need an explicit ATC clearance. Merely establishing radio contact or hearing your call sign does not authorize entry.
concepts.apply: Listen for words such as “Cleared into the Bravo” before crossing its boundary.

concepts.title: Pilot and aircraft qualifications
concepts.explain: Class B operations have specific pilot qualification, radio, transponder and ADS-B requirements, with limited exceptions.
concepts.apply: Confirm your qualifications and equipment before requesting entry.

concepts.title: Read each shelf
concepts.explain: Class B airspace may have different top and bottom altitudes across short distances.
concepts.apply: Trace the complete lateral route and altitude along each segment.

check.question: What must you receive before entering Class B?
check.explanation: Class B normally requires an explicit entry clearance.

concepts.title: Core and shelf
concepts.explain: Class C usually has a surface area around a primary airport and an outer shelf, commonly reaching 4,000 feet above the airport elevation.
concepts.apply: Pay attention to the published floor and ceiling instead of assuming a universal cylinder.

concepts.title: Two-way communications
concepts.explain: Establish two-way radio communications with ATC before entering Class C. A response using your aircraft identification generally establishes communication unless told to remain outside.
concepts.apply: If ATC replies only “Aircraft calling, standby,” with no identification, communication is not yet established.

concepts.title: Not the same as Class B
concepts.explain: Class C normally does not require the same explicit “cleared into” phrase as Class B; it still requires proper two-way communication.
concepts.apply: Keep the Class B versus Class C entry distinction clear.

concepts.title: Equipment
concepts.explain: Appropriate transponder and ADS-B Out rules may apply in Class C and surrounding designated airspace.
concepts.apply: Check 14 CFR 91.215 and 91.225 plus any authorized deviations.

check.question: ATC says “Aircraft calling, standby” without your identification. Class C entry?
check.explanation: Communication must be established using aircraft identification, subject to ATC instructions.

concepts.title: Typical shape
concepts.explain: Class D usually surrounds airports with operating control towers and typically extends to about 2,500 feet above the airport elevation, as individually published.
concepts.apply: The sectional chart gives the specific Class D ceiling.

concepts.title: Establish communications
concepts.explain: Two-way communication with the operating tower is required before Class D entry.
concepts.apply: Do not cross the boundary until the controller has acknowledged your aircraft identification.

concepts.title: Tower hours matter
concepts.explain: When the tower closes, the surface airspace classification may change according to published notes.
concepts.apply: Check the Chart Supplement and current NOTAMs for the airport’s operating hours.

concepts.title: Arrival procedures
concepts.explain: Communications are necessary, but you still have to follow pattern, runway, ATC and see-and-avoid requirements.
concepts.apply: Stay outside when told to remain clear of Class D.

check.question: What is typically necessary before Class D entry?
options: A filed IFR flight plan for all VFR arrivals

title: Class E: Controlled but Often Invisible

concepts.title: What Class E means
concepts.explain: Class E is controlled airspace that is not Class A, B, C or D. It includes broad en route areas and many transition areas.
concepts.apply: No visible tower does not mean uncontrolled airspace.

concepts.title: Variable floors
concepts.explain: Class E often begins at 700 or 1,200 feet AGL, sometimes at the surface or at specified MSL levels. Where not otherwise designated, Class E generally starts at 14,500 feet MSL.
concepts.apply: Read magenta and blue airspace boundary markings correctly.

concepts.title: VFR versus IFR
concepts.explain: Basic VFR flight does not usually need an ATC clearance solely to be in Class E, but appropriate VFR weather minima still apply. IFR aircraft use clearances and ATC services.
concepts.apply: Do not confuse controlled airspace with mandatory radio contact for ordinary VFR everywhere.

concepts.title: Higher altitudes
concepts.explain: Class E also includes airspace above FL600.
concepts.apply: The airspace profile extends beyond the typical low-altitude sectional view.

check.question: Class E generally means...
options: Controlled airspace other than A through D
Airspace with no VFR weather minima
check.explanation: Class E is controlled and carries operating rules.

concepts.title: What Class G is
concepts.explain: Class G is airspace that has not been designated as Class A, B, C, D or E, usually from the surface to the overlying Class E floor.
concepts.apply: For a local flight, identify where Class G ends vertically.

concepts.title: Uncontrolled does not mean rule-free
concepts.explain: General flight rules, minimum safe altitudes, right-of-way, weather minimums and other regulations still apply in Class G.
concepts.apply: Class G is not permission to fly without checking conditions or restrictions.

concepts.title: Towered airports can be in Class G
concepts.explain: Some airports may have an operating tower even though their surrounding airspace is Class G; tower communication requirements can still apply.
concepts.apply: The presence of Class G does not eliminate airport-specific rules.

concepts.title: VFR minima vary
concepts.explain: Class G VFR visibility and cloud-clearance requirements vary with altitude, time of day and location.
concepts.apply: Use the full FAA minimums table, not one memorized number for every Class G situation.

check.question: Does Class G mean no flight rules apply?
check.explanation: Class G is uncontrolled but general operating rules still apply.

concepts.title: Prohibited areas
concepts.explain: Prohibited areas identify airspace where flight is forbidden without specific authorization, often for security reasons. They are labeled with a P number.
concepts.apply: Avoid a prohibited area when planning; do not treat it like a voluntary caution area.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 15 — Figure 15-3

concepts.title: Restricted areas
concepts.explain: Restricted areas may contain hazardous operations. Their use and activation can vary, and entry is subject to applicable restrictions and controlling-agency procedures.
concepts.apply: Contact the controlling agency or appropriate ATC facility and verify status before an affected route.

concepts.title: Read airspace labels
concepts.explain: Charts depict special-use area boundaries, identification, controlling agencies and altitude information, often with details in accompanying tables.
concepts.apply: The lateral outline alone will not tell you whether your altitude intersects the area.

concepts.title: Do not infer inactivity
concepts.explain: A quiet frequency or apparent lack of activity does not prove that restricted airspace is inactive.
concepts.apply: Use authoritative, current status information.

check.question: Which area is generally not entered without special authorization?
check.explanation: Prohibited areas ban flight except as specifically authorized.

title: MOAs, Alert Areas and Military Routes

concepts.title: Military Operations Areas
concepts.explain: MOAs separate certain military training activities from IFR traffic. VFR flight may be permitted, but military activity may be fast and unpredictable.
concepts.apply: Check published times, altitudes and status before crossing a MOA.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 15 — Figure 15-5

concepts.title: Alert areas
concepts.explain: Alert areas signal high-volume pilot training or unusual aerial activity. Pilots share responsibility for collision avoidance.
concepts.apply: Expect traffic that may be maneuvering or difficult to see.

concepts.title: Military training routes
concepts.explain: Military training routes (MTRs), marked IR or VR, may support high-speed military flight at low altitudes.
concepts.apply: Plan with current route information and enhance traffic scanning.

concepts.title: Controlled firing areas
concepts.explain: Controlled firing areas cease hazardous operations when a spotter detects an approaching aircraft; they are not routinely charted like restricted areas.
concepts.apply: Do not assume all hazardous military activities are depicted the same way.

check.question: Which statement about MOAs is best?
options: VFR flight may be legal but requires risk awareness
They are identical to prohibited areas
check.explanation: A MOA flags military operations and must be assessed for risk.

concepts.title: Temporary Flight Restrictions
concepts.explain: TFRs may be issued for disaster relief, major events, security and other reasons. Their dimensions and effective times change.
concepts.apply: Check current FAA NOTAM/TFR information close to departure and again before entering the area.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 15 — Figure 15-7

concepts.title: National security and wildlife areas
concepts.explain: National security areas and special conservation requests may warrant avoidance; actual restrictions depend on current published requirements.
concepts.apply: Distinguish “requested to avoid” from legally binding entry restrictions.

concepts.title: TRSAs
concepts.explain: Terminal radar service areas provide radar services to participating pilots; participation is generally voluntary for VFR aircraft except in underlying airspace with its own requirements.
concepts.apply: A TRSA boundary is not the same as a Class B clearance requirement.

concepts.title: ADIZ
concepts.explain: Air Defense Identification Zones have identification, flight-plan and communication rules for relevant operations.
concepts.apply: Special routing near the coast or border may need additional preparations.

check.question: Why check TFRs near flight time?
options: They appear only in printed textbooks
They never apply to VFR flights
check.explanation: TFRs may be added or modified on short notice.

concepts.title: Two independent tests
concepts.explain: VFR minima often specify both flight visibility and distance from clouds. Meeting visibility alone is not enough.
concepts.apply: Cross-check both values for your airspace class and altitude.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 15 — Figure 15-8

concepts.title: Class B versus C/D/E
concepts.explain: Class B basic VFR typically uses three statute miles visibility and clear of clouds; Class C, D and much of Class E generally require three miles plus 500 below, 1,000 above and 2,000 horizontal.
concepts.apply: Do not apply Class B “clear of clouds” rules in Class C.

concepts.title: Higher-altitude minima
concepts.explain: At or above 10,000 feet MSL, more stringent visibility and cloud distances generally apply in Class E and Class G.
concepts.apply: Use the table for the specific altitude and airspace rather than assuming 3-152 everywhere.

concepts.title: Class G day versus night
concepts.explain: Class G minima differ by day and night, and by proximity to the surface and other criteria.
concepts.apply: The full chart is the safest study reference for this complex topic.

concepts.title: Special VFR
concepts.explain: Special VFR may be possible with ATC authorization in eligible surface areas and requires applicable visibility and cloud conditions; nighttime has additional qualifications/equipment for airplanes.
concepts.apply: An SVFR clearance is not automatic and cannot waive a separate airspace entry rule.

check.question: VFR weather planning requires checking...
options: Visibility and cloud separation as applicable
check.explanation: Both visibility and cloud clearance limits matter.

concepts.title: Requirements are layered
concepts.explain: A flight may need a radio, transponder, ADS-B Out or specific pilot qualification based on airspace and operation. Requirements may apply in a Mode C veil even outside Class B itself.
concepts.apply: Check the aircraft equipment and certification separately from the airspace class.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 15 — Figure 15-9

concepts.title: Class B needs clearance
concepts.explain: An acknowledgement of your aircraft identification is not equivalent to a Class B clearance.
concepts.apply: Request and receive explicit authorization before entry.

concepts.title: Class C and D need communication
concepts.explain: Class C and D generally require established two-way ATC radio communications before entry.
concepts.apply: Listen for your callsign and any instruction to remain outside.

concepts.title: Equipment-rule exceptions
concepts.explain: Transponder and ADS-B rules contain defined exemptions and authorized deviations.
concepts.apply: Never assume that absence of a tower exempts an aircraft from surveillance equipment rules.

check.question: A transponder rule may apply outside Class B itself because of...
options: The color of the sectional chart
check.explanation: Equipment obligations can extend beyond a class boundary.

concepts.title: Begin with the route
concepts.explain: Locate your departure point, checkpoints, destination and planned altitudes along the route.
concepts.apply: A route with two waypoints can still cross multiple shelf boundaries.

image.caption: FAA Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 15 — Figure 15-1

concepts.title: Read the vertical limits
concepts.explain: Decode each charted airspace floor and ceiling; pay attention to MSL versus AGL and surface areas.
concepts.apply: Trace climb and descent segments as carefully as cruise.

concepts.title: Cross-check special areas
concepts.explain: Look for prohibited/restricted areas, MOAs, alert areas, military training routes and active TFRs.
concepts.apply: A normal sectional can be outdated for a TFR created today.

concepts.title: Make a brief before flying
concepts.explain: For each transition, know what to request, when to call, what minimums apply and what equipment must be operating.
concepts.apply: Prepare an alternate path if ATC cannot accommodate a request.

check.question: What is essential for a route below a Class B shelf?
options: Check shelf floor and flight altitude
Assume all shelves start at the surface
check.explanation: A shelf floor, altitude and equipment restrictions must all be checked.

concepts.title: Scenario setup
concepts.explain: A private pilot plans a day VFR flight under a Class B shelf, through a Class C outer shelf, past a MOA, and into a Class D airport.
concepts.apply: Mark each crossing by location and altitude before the flight.

concepts.title: Class B segment
concepts.explain: Staying below the Class B shelf can avoid Class B entry, but other equipment rules such as the Mode C veil and ADS-B coverage may still apply.
concepts.apply: Verify both chart altitude and surveillance requirements.

concepts.title: Class C transition
concepts.explain: Before entering the Class C outer shelf, establish two-way communication with the appropriate facility.
concepts.apply: If told to remain outside, stay clear and request a revised route.

concepts.title: MOA crossing
concepts.explain: Check whether the military operations area is active, the altitude range and whether a safer route is available.
concepts.apply: A VFR pilot may be legal to enter yet still choose an alternate route for risk reduction.

concepts.title: Class D arrival
concepts.explain: Contact the tower early enough to establish communications before Class D entry, then follow the applicable arrival and runway instructions.
concepts.apply: A good airspace plan connects charts, weather minima, communications and judgment.

check.question: Your planned route crosses active military training, Class C and Class D. Best preparation?
options: Plan status checks and communication points
Ignore the MOA because it is VFR
Talk only to the destination tower
check.explanation: Proactive route and communications planning reduces risk.
